title: Adwind_jRAT_Incident_Response_Scenario_f3e
description: Investigate and respond to a security incident involving the Adwind/jRAT trojan on a victim host.
outcomes: Usage of systemctl for service and timer enumeration
Correlating suspicious activity with malware components

levels.title: Introduction
levels.content: The victim host in your network has exhibited unusual behavior, including unexpected network connections and potential unauthorized access. Your task is to investigate and respond to this security incident involving the Adwind/jRAT trojan. This scenario will help you develop skills in identifying and mitigating malware infections, specifically focusing on the Adwind/jRAT trojan. Adwind/jRAT is a cross-platform Java-based Remote Access Trojan (RAT) that allows attackers to control infected systems remotely. It is often used for data theft, keylogging, and other malicious activities. Typical behaviors include unexpected network connections, unauthorized access, and the presence of hidden files or services.

levels.title: Investigate Suspicious Services
levels.content: Investigate the victim host for unauthorized or suspicious services running on the system. Enumerate running services and distinguish legitimate services from trojan-related services.
levels.solution: Check the status of all services and look for any that appear unusual or unauthorized. Use commands like `systemctl list-units --type=service` to list all services and `systemctl status <service_name>` to check the status of specific services. The suspicious service related to the Adwind/jRAT trojan is 'network-diagnostics.service'. The flag type is a service name.

hints.title: Conceptual Hint
hints.content: Start by understanding the types of services that might be running on the system and how they can be enumerated.

hints.title: Methodology Hint
hints.content: Use systemctl commands to list and check the status of services. Focus on services that appear unusual or unauthorized.

hints.title: Command Hint
hints.content: Use commands like `systemctl list-units --type=service` to list all services and `systemctl status <service_name>` to check the status of specific services. Look for services named 'network-diagnostics.service' or similar.

levels.title: Identify Scheduled Task or Timer
levels.content: Determine whether a scheduled task or timer is responsible for automatically executing the malware. Identify scheduled execution persistence mechanisms (e.g., cron, systemd timers, Windows Scheduled Tasks).
levels.solution: Examine the systemd timers and services to find any that might be related to the malware. Use commands like `systemctl list-timers` to list all timers and `systemctl status <timer_name>` to check the status of specific timers. The scheduled timer related to the Adwind/jRAT trojan is 'network-diagnostics.timer'. The flag type is a timer name.

hints.title: Conceptual Hint
hints.content: Understand the concept of scheduled tasks and timers, and how they can be used to persistently execute malware.

hints.title: Methodology Hint
hints.content: Use systemctl commands to list and check the status of timers. Focus on timers that appear unusual or unauthorized.

hints.title: Command Hint
hints.content: Use commands like `systemctl list-timers` to list all timers and `systemctl status <timer_name>` to check the status of specific timers. Look for timers named 'network-diagnostics.timer' or similar.

levels.title: Locate Malware Files
levels.content: Locate files installed by the malware on the compromised host. Correlate suspicious activity with files introduced by the trojan.
levels.solution: Search for hidden directories and files that might contain malware components or collected data. Use commands like `find / -type d -name '.*' 2>/dev/null` to find hidden directories and `find / -type f -name '.*' 2>/dev/null` to find hidden files. The malware file related to the Adwind/jRAT trojan is '/usr/local/lib/.netd/revshell.sh'. The flag type is a file path.

hints.title: Conceptual Hint
hints.content: Understand the importance of locating hidden directories and files that might contain malware components or collected data.

hints.title: Methodology Hint
hints.content: Use find commands to search for hidden directories and files. Focus on directories and files that appear unusual or unauthorized.

hints.title: Command Hint
hints.content: Use commands like `find / -type d -name '.*' 2>/dev/null` to find hidden directories and `find / -type f -name '.*' 2>/dev/null` to find hidden files. Look for files named 'revshell.sh' or similar.
